contentGapNotes: No discussion of how Buffer's visual design changes (layout shift from centered to multi-column, dark announcement bar, refined geometric accents) may have independently affected conversion or engagement — the article focuses on messaging and navigation but not visual hierarchy or design psychology

No mention of how organic search behavior may have shifted between 2019 and 2026 (e.g., rise of platform-specific searches, creator-focused keywords), which would explain why platform-specific nav links make sense now but wouldn't have in 2019
Limited coverage of mobile homepage changes — all snapshots appear desktop-focused; mobile layout decisions may differ meaningfully and deserve a separate section

No data on whether Buffer's actual conversion rate, bounce rate, or time-on-page changed with each redesign — the article infers intent from design changes but doesn't acknowledge the absence of outcome metrics

Missing context on Buffer's product roadmap or feature releases during this period — did the addition of eight products (Publish, Create, Community, Analyze, Collaborate, Mobile app, Start page, AI assistant) happen before or after the homepage redesign?

No discussion of how competitor actions (Hootsuite, Sprout Social pricing, new entrants in creator scheduling) may have triggered specific messaging changes — only general reference to 'crowded landscape'
requiredFixes: Add a disclaimer or caveat near the opening that states: 'This teardown analyzes visible design and messaging changes. Without access to Buffer's traffic, conversion, or engagement metrics, we cannot claim that these changes improved or harmed performance. The analysis suggests strategic intent; it does not prove results.' This prevents readers from treating observed changes as proven successes.

Clarify the timeline: the article title says '7 years' (2019–2026) but lists only 5 snapshots. If some years are missing, explain why (e.g., 'no major visible changes' or 'snapshots selected for strategic shifts'). If the timeline is inaccurate, correct it.

In the 'Why the homepage changed' section, add a note that the competitive context described (Hootsuite, Sprout Social moves) is inferred from design changes, not sourced from Buffer's public statements. Avoid implying direct causation without evidence.

Include a subsection on 'what this means for paid ad landing pages' — many SaaS teams run different homepages for organic vs. paid audiences; Buffer's brand-name H1 may work differently depending on traffic source

Strengthen the secondary keyword 'SaaS homepage CRO teardown' by adding a sentence early in the intro that positions this article within a broader CRO teardown series or framework (e.g., 'This is the ninth in our SaaS homepage CRO teardown series')

In the final 'Brand name as H1' section, add a worked example: 'If your brand autocomplete shows [screenshot or example], your audience is ready for a brand-only H1. If it shows [other example], keep the benefit headline.' Concrete search results would strengthen this decision framework.
